title: Back in Chicago with Schilling, then rebuilding for Tommy Thomas
summary: In 1916 band members walked out; Loyacano brought his brother Jack and others up from New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: No head. But what year do you think that was? About 1915? No, that was 16. Yeah. Then,

I went back to Chicago with Happy Shillin. There's Happy Shillin and Georgie Borth, Johnny Fisher, and I and Johnny, let's say I think it was Johnny Frisco, who was the drummer. No, Williams was the drummer in that outfit. Then we went to work in a place called the Orsonia. Mike Fritzlant's joint on, it was all Madison near Paulina. And we did all right there until they booted us out of there. So we went down to the corner and went to work for Tommy Thomas. And everybody was well satisfied. You see, uh, Brown's band had already paved the way. And then the Dixieland band came in. Incidentally, that's where they got the name from the original Dixieland band, because everybody said, there's another Dixieland band in town. They worked on 35th Street, Shillin. And, uh, it wasn't hard to break through in, uh, 1916. I'm pretty sure it was 16. Well, I went back there with the other band, with Shillin. So we lived on Warren Avenue in Paulina. One morning I got up, wasn't it, it was about 10 o'clock, because they closed up at one o'clock. They had a one o'clock closing law in Chicago. And a woman sitting on the front porch that I had talked with told me, says, uh, what happened? Did you boys finish up over at the corner? I said, not that I know of. She said, well, three of your boys are gone. And they were. And they were. Happy Shillin. Happy Shillin. And left? Just picked up and left. Told, didn't even tell me.
Who was managing that, uh? Happy Shillin. He and Fisher left? And, uh, Freddie Williams. Uh-huh.

Piano player Williams? Yeah. And, uh. Wanted to come back to New Orleans? Uh, no, Williams was a drummer. Yeah, they came back. Williams, uh. You were playing the piano with them still? Yeah. Uh-huh. Georgie Barth was a trumpet player. So I, I looked around and I asked the woman landlady, let's take a look at their room. And sure enough, so I went over to the cafe and the colored fella cleaning up. And I asked him, he said, oh, he come in, took the drums and everything. I didn't know a thing about it. So I was hooked. I went to see Tommy Thomas. So Tommy said, well, what are we going to do? I said, I don't know. I said, I just can't go out in the park and pick up men. But I said, if we can get along for tonight and tomorrow night, I feel confident. What did you have? Uh, did you have anybody? Uh, yeah,
just two of them left? Oh, no, just me. Yeah, there are three or four of them at Goldman? Sure. All the band left

but me. Left me high and dry. So I told him in a couple of nights, I can get you another Dixieland band. I feel confident that I can. So I got in touch with my brother Jack and told him to get a hold of some of the fellas that he thought could play. So he got a hold of four other guys and I wired them the money and they caught the train and came on. A fella named Weber played clarinet. Freddie New Roth played trumpet. Red Rolling played clarinet later. Jack played trombone. And Johnny Frisco played drums and I played piano. So he was only without his Dixieland music for two nights and luckily they started on a Friday. The two big nights were yet to come, see. So he really didn't lose anything. Well, you all worked there how long? Oh, for Tommy, we worked there a long while. I guess about, uh, year and a half worked for Tommy. You weren't married then, huh? No. Then along came the war. I'll hold it right there.
